headline: Hot U.S. inflation sends a shock through Asian technology markets
dek: The United States, China, Japan, and South Korea are responding differently to renewed interest-rate fears and doubts about the AI investment boom.
story_title: One inflation report, four different economic reactions
story_html:
United States 🇺🇸 — September consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% year on year, while core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 2.6%. The figures were above expectations and revived speculation that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again at its October 27–28 meeting. Markets had previously leaned toward a pause, but traders rapidly increased the implied probability of another hike. The immediate effect was especially severe in technology shares, whose valuations depend heavily on expectations of strong future growth.

China 🇨🇳 — China has not escaped the global risk-off mood, but its response has been less dramatic. The Shanghai Composite fell about 1.6% on October 15, as investors worried that higher U.S. rates could strengthen the dollar and encourage capital to move toward American assets. However, domestic liquidity remains relatively supportive, and September exports surged 36.3% from a year earlier. That combination gives Chinese equities a partial cushion, although it also intensifies international criticism of China’s large trade surplus and manufacturing capacity.

Japan 🇯🇵 — Japanese shares were hit harder because the market is highly exposed to global technology companies, exporters, and changes in the yen. The Nikkei 225 fell almost 5% on October 15 as investors reassessed the value of semiconductor and AI-related companies. A stronger dollar can benefit Japanese exporters, but higher U.S. yields also tighten global financial conditions and make richly valued growth stocks less attractive. Japan therefore faces a delicate balance: a weaker yen may support corporate earnings, while volatile markets can damage household and business confidence.

South Korea 🇰🇷 — Korea suffered the sharpest equity-market reaction among the four economies. The KOSPI fell 7.57% and temporarily triggered a circuit breaker, while Samsung Electronics and SK hynix dropped sharply. The sell-off reflected both the global rise in borrowing costs and doubts about whether enormous AI infrastructure spending will generate sufficient profits. Because semiconductors account for a large share of Korean exports and market capitalization, Korea is particularly sensitive to changes in technology sentiment. Foreign investors also sold heavily, pushing the won lower against the dollar.

The connecting theme is not a uniform economic downturn but the repricing of growth. When investors expect interest rates to remain higher, future corporate profits are worth less today. That mechanism hits speculative technology shares first, then spreads through currencies, capital flows, and export economies. China appears relatively insulated because of domestic policy support, while Japan and South Korea are more exposed to the semiconductor cycle. The United States remains the source of the shock—but its own consumers and policymakers must now decide how much economic strength is compatible with price stability. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/fed-rate-hike-call-seen-tight-as-inflation-heats-up-ce785dd2df8eff2d?utm_source=openai))
b2_summary: U.S. inflation rose faster than expected in September, making investors think the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again. Higher rates usually reduce the value of future company profits, so technology and AI shares suffered. South Korea was hit hardest: the KOSPI fell 7.57%, and trading was temporarily stopped. Japan’s Nikkei also dropped sharply. China’s market declined less because domestic policy remains supportive, while strong exports provided some protection. The common theme is the repricing of high-growth assets when borrowing costs may stay higher for longer.

concept.title: Why do higher interest rates hurt growth stocks?
concept.explanation: A growth company’s value depends heavily on profits expected many years in the future. When interest rates rise, those future profits are discounted more heavily, so their value today falls. This is why technology and AI shares can decline sharply even when the companies’ current sales remain strong.

quiz.question: Why was South Korea especially vulnerable to the global technology sell-off?
options: Its economy and stock market are heavily exposed to semiconductors.
Its central bank immediately cut interest rates to zero.
Its exports are almost entirely made up of agricultural products.
quiz.explanation: Semiconductors represent a major share of South Korea’s exports and market capitalization, making the country highly sensitive to changes in technology sentiment and global borrowing costs.

one_sentence: When U.S. inflation changes the path of interest rates, the repricing can travel across borders faster than the goods being traded.
